item.title: Elder-care robots need to start with people
item.description: Elder-care robots need to start with people Imagine the future of elder care and it is easy to envision a robot. Perhaps it is humanoid, standing patiently beside an old person, helping the senior get out of bed, carrying a tray, cleaning the floor or leading a morning exercise session. In a country where the population is growing older and families are getting smaller, this image has obvious appeal. China is turning that vision into a thriving industry. The country's aging population has created a vast market called the "silver economy", attracting attention from investors and technology companies. Rehabilitation robots help people with limited mobility exercise, while transfer robots handle the heavy lifting that exhausts caregivers. Other machines clean homes, provide entertainment, play sports with older people or offer massage and other wellness services. While technology is advancing rapidly, the question is whether our understanding of old age is moving in tandem. For years, making technology "age-friendly" meant modifying existing products to make them less challenging for elderly users — larger fonts, fewer buttons, higher volume. Essentially, products designed for everyone else were slightly adjusted before being handed to seniors. This approach now looks outdated. Seniors don't necessarily need simplified versions of products designed for 30-year-olds. They may need entirely different products. Consider the difference between making a robot easy to operate and making it truly useful in an elderly person's daily life. An old person may move more slowly, tire more easily or have difficulty with certain kinds of instructions. A caregiver may perform physically demanding tasks several times in a day. A robot that ignores these realities may work perfectly in a laboratory and still fail in a home. This is where the industry faces a less glamorous challenge than artificial intelligence or advanced robotics: listening. Surprisingly, we still lack systematic knowledge about what seniors and their caregivers actually need from machines. Research on everyday care scenarios is limited, and very few engineers have a deep understanding of aging. There is a simple reason for this: we have all been young, but nobody experiences old age until they reach it. That creates a peculiar blind spot in product design. Engineers can study how a robot moves, how much weight it can carry and how accurately it recognizes an object. It is much harder to teach a machine — or its designer — what it feels like to hesitate before standing up from a chair, to feel embarrassed about needing help, or to rely on someone for basic mobility. This is why elder-care robotics needs more than better hardware. It demands better fieldwork. A robot intended for a nursing home should not be treated as the one intended for a family apartment. Companies should spend more time observing actual care delivery, breaking down everyday tasks into their smallest movements and talking to both older people and caregivers. Surveys and interviews are important, but so is observing how people get through an ordinary day. The fundamental questions for companies should be: Who will use this machine? What problem will the robot address? What makes that problem challenging? Is a robot really the best solution? Answering these questions could save the industry from the expensive mistake of producing impressive machines that search for a market. Getting a robot into production is only half the job. An elder-care robot is not a refrigerator that can be delivered, plugged in and forgotten. It enters a person's home, sometimes at a moment of considerable physical vulnerability. An old person needs to know how to use it, caregivers need to know how to maintain it and homes and nursing facilities may need rearranging for the machine to function safely. Then there is the human aspect. As robots become more capable, some families may start relying on them for tasks once performed by relatives or professional caregivers. This can be useful, but it can also be unsettling. A machine can remind an old person to take a walk, assist with an exercise routine, or carry something too heavy to lift. But it should not pretend to be a daughter, a son, a nurse or a friend. This distinction matters because elder care is not just about physical tasks. It is also about dignity, reassurance and human interaction. The industry will need clear guidelines on privacy, data and the limits of what machines do. A robot operating in someone's bedroom or living room is not merely an appliance. It has access to intimate details of a person's life. This is not an argument against robots. In fact, it is quite the opposite. If designed well, robots could make an enormous difference, particularly as societies struggle with fewer caregivers and longer life spans. But the industry should resist measuring progress by how humanlike a robot looks or how many tasks it can perform. The more meaningful question is a simpler one: Does the robot make an old person's day easier? If the answer is yes, elder-care robots have a promising future. The most successful ones will not be the machines that replace people. They will be the ones that quietly take the hardest jobs off their hands, giving caregivers more time to care — and seniors more time to live their lives on their own terms. The author is deputy head of the Aging Society Research Center at the Pangoal Institution. The views don't necessarily reflect those of China Daily. item.title: More firms to benefit from AEO program
item.description: More firms to benefit from AEO program Importance of certification for smoother cross-border trade highlighted at seminar China will expand its pool of companies certified under the Authorized Economic Operator program and broaden mutual recognition arrangements with Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation economies to help more businesses benefit from streamlined cross-border trade procedures, customs officials said on Wednesday. Speaking at a seminar organized by the General Administration of Customs during the ongoing third APEC Senior Officials' Meeting in Dalian, Liaoning province, they said these measures would make AEO certification a stronger tool for supporting smaller businesses, boosting participation in trade and fostering a more open, inclusive and resilient Asia-Pacific trading environment. The AEO program, promoted by the World Customs Organization, is designed to strengthen international supply chain security and facilitate the movement of legitimate goods. Under the program, customs authorities work with businesses to streamline customs procedures and improve the efficiency of international trade. Lazzat Daniyarova, a technical officer at the Brussels-based World Customs Organization, said that integrating more small- and medium-sized enterprises into AEO programs would make the system more inclusive and give smaller businesses greater access to secure trade and sustainable growth opportunities. Lin Jiantian, director of the GAC's department of enterprise management and audit-based control, said China will pursue mutual AEO recognition with more economies to enable businesses across the Asia-Pacific to benefit from faster and more efficient customs clearance. All APEC economies except Papua New Guinea have AEO programs in place. China has established mutual recognition arrangements with 10 of them, including Australia, Singapore and South Korea. China's AEO-certified companies recorded 16.76 trillion yuan ($2.49 trillion) in foreign trade in the first seven months of 2026, accounting for 44.2 percent of the country's total, up 5.77 percentage points from a year earlier. Meanwhile, their trade with other APEC economies rose 21.87 percent year-on-year to 9.19 trillion yuan. The GAC said Chinese customs officials will also hold discussions with their counterparts from Malaysia, Indonesia and Vietnam, as well as representatives of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Secretariat, to accelerate AEO mutual recognition and identify priorities for the next phase of cooperation. Olgun Basel, supply chain director at Einhell Germany AG, a German industrial goods trading company based in Shanghai, said the company's import clearance times have fallen by 80 percent since it gained AEO certification in February. Basel said that preparing for AEO certification also prompted the company to improve internal controls, documentation and risk management, helping to optimize its operations and build trust with customers in overseas markets. China had more than 15,450 AEO-certified companies as of the end of July and has signed 34 mutual recognition agreements covering 60 countries and regions. China is hosting the third APEC Senior Officials' Meeting in Dalian from Monday through Aug 28, said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

item.title: US national debt tops $40 trillion for first time
item.description: US national debt tops $40 trillion for first time in history WASHINGTON -- The US national debt has surpassed $40 trillion for the first time in history, according to data released by the Treasury Department on Wednesday. The data shows that debt held by the public and intragovernmental holdings stood at $32.266 trillion and $7.782 trillion, respectively, bringing total public debt outstanding to $40.047 trillion as of Tuesday. The milestone, reached months earlier than expected, reflects the US federal government's persistent budget deficits, as spending continues to exceed revenue, adding to the national debt. The federal government has spent trillions of dollars in response to the COVID-19 pandemic and subsequently pursued tax cuts and increased military spending. As a result, US federal debt has grown rapidly in recent years, raising concerns in the bond market and pushing Treasury yields higher. Rising interest payments have further driven up the total size of the national debt. A monthly report from the Treasury Department shows that the federal government recorded a fiscal deficit of $1.367 trillion in the first nine months of fiscal year 2026, which began on Oct 1, 2025. During that period, net interest payments totaled $827 billion, exceeding defense spending of $713 billion and ranking second only to social security spending, which amounted to $1.244 trillion. US federal government debt surpassed $30 trillion in January 2022, exceeded $39 trillion in March 2026, and hit $39.7 trillion in July 2026. Local media described the national debt surpassing $40 trillion as an ominous milestone for an economy resting on an increasingly shaky fiscal foundation. Warning signs are flashing "with debt held by the public recently exceeding the size of our economy, the deficit-to-GDP ratio running twice as high as where it should be, and interest costs exceeding our national defense budget," Maya MacGuineas, president of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget, said Wednesday in a statement. "Forty trillion dollars of debt doesn't exist solely on the government's ledgers; it is felt throughout the economy and finds its way to the pocketbooks of people one way or another," MacGuineas said. "The more we borrow, the more we exacerbate inflation, squeeze out other priorities in the budget, and leave ourselves vulnerable to emergencies at home and turmoil abroad." "Our current fiscal trajectory is plainly unsustainable," said Margaret Spellings, president and CEO of the Bipartisan Policy Center. "Even in the rosiest scenarios, we're speeding toward a cliff and refusing to turn the wheel." "Federal debt is already raising the cost of living and choking out other spending and investment, threatening our economy and Americans' long-term prosperity," she added. "Forty trillion dollars should be a wake-up call. But neither Congress nor the president have a credible plan to stop it from growing," said Carolyn Bourdeaux, executive director of Concord Coalition and Concord Action Fund. "We owe the next generation better than this crushing debt and another hollow promise that someone else will deal with it later." In a statement responding to the troubling milestone, White House spokesman Kush Desai said US President Donald Trump had pledged to clean up former President Joe Biden's fiscal mismanagement. "That's why the Trump administration has been focused on slashing waste, fraud, and abuse in federal spending while accelerating economic growth to get America's debt-to-GDP ratio trending in the right direction again."

item.title: EU cross-border probe unfair: China
item.description: EU cross-border probe unfair: China China has determined that certain cross-border investigative measures taken by the European Union in its foreign subsidy probe into e-commerce giant JD.com constitute improper extraterritorial jurisdiction and has barred organizations and individuals from complying with or assisting in their implementation, the Ministry of Justice said on Wednesday. The ministry said it made the determination jointly with the Ministry of Commerce and other departments under China's regulations on countering improper extraterritorial jurisdiction. The decision took effect upon its release on Wednesday. The move concerns the EU's investigation of JD.com under its Foreign Subsidies Regulation, or FSR, which Chinese authorities said involved demands for extensive and unnecessary information from Chinese entities concerning activities within China. A Ministry of Justice spokesperson said in a written response that the requests imposed improper requirements on Chinese entities and seriously undermined the rule of law in international affairs. It urged the EU to correct its approach, stop what it described as abuse of the foreign subsidy investigation mechanism, and provide a fair, impartial and predictable business environment for companies investing and operating in Europe. "If the EU persists in its approach, China will firmly take countermeasures in accordance with the law," the spokesperson said. The investigation is linked to JD.com's proposed acquisition of German consumer electronics retailer Ceconomy AG, which operates the MediaMarkt and Saturn brands across several EU member states. JD.com's board approved the proposed acquisition in July 2025 in a deal valued at about $2.5 billion. The transaction was initially expected to close in the first half of 2026 but has been delayed amid regulatory reviews, including the EU's FSR investigation. Germany's Federal Cartel Office approved the deal in September 2025, concluding that the companies had little competitive overlap and that the transaction did not raise significant antitrust concerns. JD.com formally notified the European Commission of the transaction on April 17 this year, and the commission opened an in-depth FSR investigation on May 28. On July 22, the commission issued a Statement of Objections to JD.com, alleging that the company may have benefited from preferential financing, tax advantages and government subsidies from China, which could have enabled it to offer a high premium for Ceconomy and thereby distort normal commercial negotiations and competition in the EU's internal market. The commission is expected to make a final decision by Oct 2. If it insists that the allegations are valid, JD.com could face significant remedies or the transaction could be blocked. It is not the first time the European Commission has used the FSR to investigate a Chinese company. In April 2024, the commission conducted unannounced inspections at branches of Nuctech, a Beijing-based supplier of security inspection equipment, in Poland and the Netherlands. On Dec 11, 2025, it formally opened an in-depth FSR investigation into the company. The investigation later expanded to demands for information on bank accounts, ownership structures and financing records within China, as well as requests for Chinese entities and banks to cooperate and provide large amounts of information that China considered unrelated to the investigation. In May, China's Ministry of Justice determined that the cross-border investigative measures taken against Chinese entities in the Nuctech case also constituted improper extraterritorial jurisdiction. It was the first application of China's regulations on countering improper extraterritorial jurisdiction after they took effect in April 2026. Under the regulations, relevant Chinese government departments may place foreign organizations or individuals that promote or participate in improper extraterritorial measures on a malicious entity list. Depending on the circumstances, authorities may also impose visa and entry restrictions, limit employment or residence in China, seize or freeze assets, and restrict the provision of data and personal information, transactions, cooperation, imports and exports, investment, or the entry of products and transportation equipment. The EU adopted the Foreign Subsidies Regulation in November 2022, and it took effect in July 2023. The regulation gives the European Commission powers to investigate financial contributions provided by non-EU governments to companies operating in Europe and can require companies to provide extensive cross-border information. yangzekun@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Qixi customs spur new consumption trends
item.description: The Qixi Festival, China's equivalent of Valentine's Day, was celebrated on Wednesday amid a surge in festive spending on cultural night tours, immersive exhibitions and intangible cultural heritage experiences. Experts said the boom reflects a deeper sense of cultural identity and evolving consumer demand. The festival, which is celebrated on the seventh day of the seventh month of the Chinese calendar, is rooted in the legend of the cowherd and the weaver girl who are separated by the Milky Way, and who meet once a year on this day, spanning the galaxy via a bridge formed by magpies. In Beijing, the Nanchizi Museum hosted the "Magpie Bridge Night in Garden" ahead of the festival, featuring a special exhibition that blended traditional astronomy with contemporary art. As part of the festivities, the museum also hosted a fan-making session for visitors on Saturday, and it has scheduled two more similar sessions on Aug 22 and 29, from 6 pm to 9 pm. In addition, a Qixi-themed intangible cultural heritage display and experience zone is open to the public at the central hall of the Chinese Traditional Culture Museum until Sunday, featuring eight traditional crafts, including incense making, tie-dye and velvet flower making. A free group wedding was also organized in Gusu district in Suzhou, Jiangsu province, with couples who had already registered their marriage earlier this year or planned to do so around Qixi taking part. The event offered services including styling, photography and a traditional Chinese ceremony. The district also rolled out a series of romantic experiences to fuel the "sweet economy", according to the Jiangsu provincial civil affairs department. At the Suji Ancient Town in Leshan, Sichuan province, meanwhile, visitors tried their hand on Saturday at a Qixi needle-threading ritual, using vintage-style needles and colored threads to take on the traditional challenge. According to the China Intangible Cultural Heritage website, which is hosted by the Chinese National Academy of Arts, Qixi is rich in folk customs. On Qixi night, women traditionally threaded silk through a row of needles by moonlight. Those who completed the task quickly were said to possess greater skill. People also stargazed, hoping to see the star-crossed lovers meet in the Milky Way or overhear their tender words beneath a melon trellis, while praying for a happy marriage. He Qicong, an associate professor at Beijing Normal University's Institute of Culture Innovation and Communication, said that traditional Chinese festivals have always provided an opportunity for people to connect with their cultural roots. "Emulating ancestors is not simply a revival of old customs and rituals," she said. "What lies beneath this cultural value system is the ancient Chinese view of life." Nighttime outings have become one of the most popular ways to celebrate Qixi. According to Tongcheng Travel, an online travel agency, evening ticket sales at domestic scenic spots on Qixi day rose more than 50 percent compared with the daily average. Falling at the tail end of the summer holidays, Qixi prompted many to head out on weekend trips. Booking data from online travel agency Tuniu showed that families accounted for more than 60 percent of those traveling over the weekend. Senior travelers also tapped into the festive momentum. Tongcheng Travel said that since the beginning of August, travelers age 55 and above have accounted for nearly 40 percent of package-tour bookings on its platform, up about 6 percentage points year-on-year. Associate professor He of Beijing Normal University said the festival resonates with people of all ages. "To young couples, Qixi symbolizes enduring love. The story is a beautiful metaphor for constancy and undivided devotion. The verse puts it well: 'If two hearts are true, why must they be together dawn and dusk?' "For women, Qixi carries the tradition of seeking skills. Women would compete in threading needles and pray to the weaver girl for wit and deft hands. That reverence for labor and craftsmanship is a shared aspiration for bettering oneself. "For the elderly, Qixi evokes a vision of family harmony. Diligence, fortitude and mutual support transform romance into a family legacy," she said. Du Jianfang, an expert at the research institute of the China International Electronic Commerce Center, told Economic Information Daily that the rise in traditional festival consumption was not simply the result of holiday promotions. "It is a long-term trend driven by cultural momentum, supply innovation and the upgrading of the consumption structure. Consumers are increasingly willing to pay a reasonable price for quality, experience, cultural meaning and emotional value," she said. lihongyang@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Guardians of China's tiger and leopard park
item.description: Guardians of China's tiger and leopard park Patrolmen take pride in safeguarding growing number of big cats in Hunchun Located at the junction of Jilin and Heilongjiang provinces, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park serves as a stable habitat for Amur leopards and Siberian tigers. Hunchun city in Yanbian Korean autonomous prefecture, Jilin, lies in the core area of the park. Since the launch of its trial phase in August 2017, hundreds of conservationists from the park's Hunchun Management and Conservation Center have been regularly conducting field patrols and scientific monitoring to protect wildlife, and traversing the dense forests to safeguard the park's inhabitants. They are rangers from the center and various protection stations, as well as ecological patrolmen recruited from nearby villages. "Patrolling mainly involves understanding the conditions in the mountains and forests and recording traces of wildlife activity," said Hao Ruiping, deputy director of the protection department at the center. "Although we now have infrared cameras, to truly understand the situation, we still need to patrol the habitats repeatedly."

item.title: 'Three-grassland' model heals Qinghai ecosystems
item.description: 'Three-grassland' model heals Qinghai ecosystems Scientific approach improves sustainability, herder incomes on 'roof of the world' High up on the "roof of the world", Chinese researchers are easing pressure on the fragile grassland ecosystems relied on for generations by nomadic Tibetan herders. To protect this high-altitude environment in the three-river-source region of Northwest China's Qinghai province, researchers have introduced more efficient varieties of forage, improved livestock management and high-tech grassland monitoring — all while increasing incomes for local herders. Known as the "water tower" of Asia, the region feeds the Yangtze, Yellow and Lancang rivers, and harbors rare plateau wildlife. But decades of overgrazing, severe weather and climate change have stripped the native grasslands, triggering soil erosion and threatening local livelihoods. To fix it, scientists at the Chinese Academy of Sciences have pioneered a "three-grassland" model that links protected wild zones, regulated grazing pastures and high-tech cultivated forage fields. Xu Shixiao, director of the Plateau Ecology Research Center at the Three-River-Source National Park Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, said the model ensures ecological conservation, sustainable livestock production and that local livelihoods are supported. "Through coordinated resource allocation and closer links between the functions of different grasslands, we hope to achieve balanced development of ecology, production and daily life," Xu said. The model is being applied in two areas. The first covers areas inside and surrounding the national park. Cultivated forage produced outside the park can be supplied to livestock, reducing grazing pressure on natural grassland within protected zones. The second includes farming-pastoral transition areas in the Guinan and Tongde counties of the Hainan Tibetan autonomous prefecture, where soil, water and climate conditions are more suitable for developing high-yield cultivated grassland. Xu said the key to addressing a long-standing constraint on plateau animal husbandry is the shortage and poor nutritional quality of forage during the cold season. A more reliable supply of high-quality feed can shorten livestock-rearing cycles, improve production efficiency and reduce reliance on natural pastures. The math behind the strategy is striking: Just 1 hectare of high-yield cultivated grass outside protected zones can spare roughly 20 hectares of natural wild pasture from overgrazing. In alpine meadow areas, reducing grazing pressure by just one sheep can ease ecological disturbance across about a hectare of natural grassland, Xu said. "This not only reduces pressure on natural pastures, but also creates more space for wildlife habitats inside the national park," he said.

item.title: See China, from Liangjiahe
item.description:
See China, from Liangjiahe Share - WeChat
British Ambassador to China Peter Wilson visited Liangjiahe village in Yan'an, Shaanxi province, where President Xi Jinping spent seven years in his youth. Wilson walked into cave dwellings and talked with locals. More than five decades later, the remote mountainous village has been greatly transformed. A visit to Liangjiahe is more than a journey into history; it is also a window into the roots of Xi's commitment to "doing practical things for the people", the Communist Party of China's people-first philosophy, and why the Party has continued to lead China forward.
